skills.name: Catch the automatic negative thought
skills.what: Automatic thoughts are the quick, often harsh thoughts that pop up right before a feeling spikes. Catching them is the first step to changing how you feel.
skills.when: When your mood drops fast and you're not sure why.
steps: Notice the feeling first: a tight chest, a sinking stomach, sudden irritation.
Ask, "What just went through my mind?"
Write the thought down word for word, even if it sounds harsh.
Label it as a thought, not a fact: "I'm having the thought that..."
skills.source: Beck, J. S. (2020). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.
skills.lens: Many of us learned to hear criticism before anyone said it. Some automatic thoughts are old messages from school, work or family that you never chose.

practice.label: What did you feel, and where in your body?
practice.hint: Tight chest, sinking stomach, sudden irritation...

practice.label: What just went through your mind?
practice.hint: Write it word for word, even if it sounds harsh.

practice.label: Now say it as a thought
practice.hint: "I'm having the thought that..."

practice.label: How do you feel now?
practice.hint: A word or two is enough.

skills.name: Thought record
skills.what: A thought record walks you from an upsetting moment to a more balanced view, one column at a time.
skills.when: After a moment that keeps replaying in your head.
steps: Write the situation: who, what, when, where.
Write the thought and how strongly you believe it, from 0 to 100.
Name the feelings and rate each one.
Write a more balanced thought that includes the full picture.
Rerate your feelings. Even a small drop counts.
skills.source: Beck, J. S. (2020). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.
skills.lens: Some thoughts are reactions to real unfairness. A balanced thought doesn't pretend racism or bias didn't happen. It helps you decide what's yours to carry.

practice.label: The situation
practice.hint: Who, what, when, where. Example: Sunday dinner, Auntie asked when I'm getting married.

practice.label: The thought, and how much you believe it (0 to 100)
practice.hint: "Everyone thinks I'm behind." 85

practice.label: Your feelings, rated 0 to 100
practice.hint: Embarrassed 70, angry 40...

practice.label: A more balanced thought
practice.hint: What's the fuller picture?

practice.label: Rerate your feelings
practice.hint: Even a small drop counts.

skills.name: Find your core belief
skills.what: Core beliefs are deep ideas about yourself, other people and the world, often formed in childhood. They drive many of your automatic thoughts.
skills.when: When the same painful theme keeps showing up in different parts of your life.
steps: Start with an automatic thought, like "I can't say no to her."
Ask, "If that were true, what would it mean about me?"
Keep asking until you reach a short, absolute belief, like "I'm only worth something when I'm useful."
Write down where you first learned it.
Look for one piece of evidence this week that the belief isn't the whole truth.
skills.source: Beck, J. S. (2020). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.
skills.lens: Beliefs like "I have to be strong" or "I have to be twice as good" often started as protection. You can honor where they came from and still decide they don't run your life now.

practice.label: Start with an automatic thought
practice.hint: Example: "I can't say no to her."

practice.label: If that were true, what would it mean about you?
practice.hint: Keep asking until you hit something short and absolute.

practice.label: The core belief
practice.hint: Example: "I'm only worth something when I'm useful."

practice.label: Where did you first learn it?
practice.hint: A home, a church, a school, a job...

practice.label: One piece of evidence this week that it isn't the whole truth
practice.hint: Small counts.

skills.name: Check the evidence
skills.what: Treat a worried thought like a claim in court. Look at what supports it and what doesn't.
skills.when: When a thought feels 100 percent true but you're not sure it is.
steps: Write the thought at the top of a page.
List the facts that support it. Facts only, no feelings.
List the facts that don't support it.
Write a conclusion a fair judge would reach.
skills.source: Beck, J. S. (2020). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: The thought
practice.hint: What is your anxious brain telling you? Example: They don't really want me around.

practice.label: Facts that support it
practice.hint: Facts only, no feelings. What would hold up in court?

practice.label: Facts that don't support it
practice.hint: What's true that the thought leaves out?

practice.label: What a fair judge would say
practice.hint: Write a conclusion that fits all the facts.

skills.name: The friend test
skills.what: We're often far kinder to friends than to ourselves. The friend test borrows that kindness.
skills.when: When you're being hard on yourself.
steps: Picture a friend you love telling you this exact thought about herself.
Write what you would say back to her.
Read it out loud to yourself.
Notice what changes in your body when you hear it.
skills.source: Beck, J. S. (2020). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: The thought you're having about yourself
practice.hint: Example: "I'm doing too much and still falling behind."

practice.label: What would you say to your best friend if she said this?
practice.hint: Write it the way you'd actually say it to her.

practice.label: Read it out loud to yourself
What changed in your body when you heard it?
practice.hint: Shoulders dropped, jaw unclenched, nothing yet...

skills.name: Small steps out of the slump
skills.what: Depression tells you to wait until you feel better to do things. Behavioral activation flips that: doing small things first helps your mood follow.
skills.when: When you've been stuck on the couch, in bed or on your phone for days.
steps: List a few activities that used to bring you pleasure or a sense of accomplishment.
Pick one that takes 10 minutes or less.
Schedule it for a specific time today.
Do it, then rate your mood before and after from 0 to 10.
skills.source: Martell, C. R., Dimidjian, S., & Herman-Dunn, R. (2010). Behavioral activation for depression: A clinician's guide. Guilford Press.

practice.label: Things that used to bring you joy or a sense of accomplishment
practice.hint: Braiding your hair, a walk, calling your cousin, cooking...

practice.label: The one that takes 10 minutes or less
When will you do it today?
practice.hint: Example: 6:30 p.m., after I eat.

practice.label: Mood after, 0 to 10
practice.hint: Any change counts.

skills.name: Scheduled worry time
skills.what: Give your worries an appointment. Postponing them to a set time helps them take up less of your day.
skills.when: When worries follow you all day or keep you up at night.
steps: Pick a 15-minute worry time, not close to bedtime.
When a worry shows up during the day, jot it down and tell yourself, "Not now. Later."
At worry time, go through the list. Problem-solve what you can.
When time is up, close the notebook and do something else.
skills.source: Borkovec, T. D., Wilkinson, L., Folensbee, R., & Lerman, C. (1983). Stimulus control applications to the treatment of worry. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 21(3), 247–251.

practice.label: Your worry time today
practice.hint: 15 minutes, not close to bedtime. Example: 5:00 p.m.

practice.label: Worries to save for later
practice.hint: Jot them down as they come. "Not now. Later."

practice.label: At worry time: what can you actually do something about?
practice.hint: One small next step for each.

practice.label: Time's up. Close it and do something else

skills.name: Test the prediction
skills.what: Anxiety makes predictions. Testing them with small experiments shows you what really happens.
skills.when: When fear is stopping you from doing something you want or need to do.
steps: Write your prediction: "If I say no, she'll be furious."
Rate how sure you are, from 0 to 100.
Plan a small, safe test.
Do it, then write what actually happened.
Ask what this tells you for next time.
skills.source: Beck, J. S. (2020). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: Your prediction
practice.hint: "If I say no, she'll be furious."

practice.label: Your small, safe test
practice.hint: What will you try, and when?

practice.label: What actually happened?
practice.hint: Come back and fill this in after.

practice.label: What does this tell you for next time?

skills.name: All-or-nothing thinking
skills.what: Seeing things in two boxes only: perfect or failure, all good or all bad.
skills.when: Sounds like: "If it's not perfect, it's a failure."
steps: Notice the trap. Name it: "All-or-nothing thinking".
Ask: "Is there a middle ground I'm skipping?"
Try instead: "It wasn't perfect, and it still got done. That counts."
skills.source: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.

practice.label: The all-or-nothing thought
practice.hint: "If it's not perfect, it's a failure."

practice.label: What's the middle ground you're skipping?
Your new thought
practice.hint: "It wasn't perfect, and it still got done. That counts."

skills.name: Catastrophizing
skills.what: Jumping to the worst possible outcome and treating it as likely.
skills.when: Sounds like: "If I mess this up, my whole career is over."
steps: Notice the trap. Name it: "Catastrophizing".
Ask: "What's the most likely outcome, not the worst one?"
Try instead: "This could be hard. I've handled hard before."
skills.source: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.

practice.label: The worst case your brain is playing
What's the most likely outcome?
practice.hint: Not the worst one. The likely one.

practice.label: A time you handled something hard
practice.hint: You've done it before.

practice.label: Your new thought
practice.hint: "This could be hard. I've handled hard before."

skills.name: Mind reading
skills.what: Assuming you know what someone else is thinking, usually something negative about you.
skills.when: Sounds like: "She didn't text back. She's upset with me."
steps: Notice the trap. Name it: "Mind reading".
Ask: "What else could explain this?"
Try instead: "I don't know what she's thinking. I can ask, or wait."
skills.source: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.

practice.label: What do you think they're thinking?
practice.hint: "She saw my text and left me on read because she's mad."

practice.label: What else could explain it?
practice.hint: List at least two other reasons.

practice.label: Your new thought
practice.hint: "I don't know what she's thinking. I can ask, or wait."

skills.name: Fortune telling
skills.what: Predicting the future as if it's already decided, usually badly.
skills.when: Sounds like: "I already know it's going to go badly."
steps: Notice the trap. Name it: "Fortune telling".
Ask: "Have I been wrong about predictions like this before?"
Try instead: "I don't know how it will go. I'll deal with what actually happens."
skills.source: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.

practice.label: Your prediction
practice.hint: "The interview is going to go terribly."

practice.label: A time you were wrong about a prediction like this
Your new thought
practice.hint: "I don't know how it will go. I'll deal with what actually happens."

skills.name: Should statements
skills.what: Holding yourself to rigid rules about how you should feel or act.
skills.when: Sounds like: "I should be able to handle all of this."
steps: Notice the trap. Name it: "Should statements".
Ask: "Whose rule is this, and is it fair?"
Try instead: "I'd like to handle more. I'm also allowed to need help."
skills.source: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.

practice.label: The should
practice.hint: "I should be able to handle all of this by myself."

practice.label: Whose rule is this, and is it fair?
practice.hint: Mama's? Church's? Work's? Yours?

practice.label: Your new thought
practice.hint: "I'd like to handle more. I'm also allowed to need help."

skills.name: Personalizing
skills.what: Taking responsibility for things that aren't about you or aren't in your control.
skills.when: Sounds like: "Everyone's in a bad mood. It must be something I did."
steps: Notice the trap. Name it: "Personalizing".
Ask: "What part of this is actually mine?"
Try instead: "Other people have their own days. I can check in without taking the blame."
skills.source: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.

practice.label: What are you blaming yourself for?
practice.hint: "My sister's in a mood. I must have done something."

practice.label: What part of this is actually yours?
practice.hint: Be honest and fair.

practice.label: Your new thought
practice.hint: "Other people have their own days. I can check in without taking the blame."

skills.name: Overgeneralizing
skills.what: Taking one event and turning it into a rule about your whole life.
skills.when: Sounds like: "This always happens to me."
steps: Notice the trap. Name it: "Overgeneralizing".
Ask: "Always? Can I think of one time it didn't?"
Try instead: "This happened this time. It doesn't define every time."
skills.source: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.

practice.label: The always or never thought
practice.hint: "I always mess things up."

practice.label: One time it didn't happen that way
Your new thought
practice.hint: "This happened this time. It doesn't define every time."

skills.name: Discounting the positive
skills.what: Brushing off good things as luck, kindness or not counting.
skills.when: Sounds like: "They only said that to be nice."
steps: Notice the trap. Name it: "Discounting the positive".
Ask: "What if the compliment was true?"
Try instead: "Thank you." Then let it land without explaining it away.
skills.source: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.

practice.label: The good thing you brushed off
practice.hint: A compliment, a win, a thank-you...

practice.label: What if it was true?
practice.hint: Write what it would mean.

practice.label: Let it land
practice.hint: Write "Thank you" and nothing else.

skills.name: Emotional reasoning
skills.what: Treating a feeling as proof that something is true.
skills.when: Sounds like: "I feel like a burden, so I must be one."
steps: Notice the trap. Name it: "Emotional reasoning".
Ask: "Is this a fact, or a feeling dressed up as one?"
Try instead: "I feel like a burden right now. Feelings aren't facts."
skills.source: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.

practice.label: The feeling that's posing as a fact
practice.hint: "I feel like a burden, so I must be one."

practice.label: What are the facts?
practice.hint: Only what a camera would see.

practice.label: Your new thought
practice.hint: "I feel like a burden right now. Feelings aren't facts."

skills.name: Labeling
skills.what: Putting a harsh label on yourself or others based on one moment.
skills.when: Sounds like: "I'm so lazy."
steps: Notice the trap. Name it: "Labeling".
Ask: "Would I say this about someone I love?"
Try instead: "I'm worn out" or "My brain works differently."
skills.source: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.

practice.label: The label you put on yourself
practice.hint: "I'm lazy." "I'm a mess."

practice.label: Would you say this about someone you love?
practice.hint: What would you say instead?

practice.label: Your new words
practice.hint: "I'm worn out." "My brain works differently."

skills.name: Wise mind
skills.what: Wise mind is the middle ground between emotion mind, where feelings drive, and reasonable mind, where only logic counts. Decisions made from wise mind tend to feel steady.
skills.when: Before a big decision, or when you feel pulled between your head and your heart.
steps: Take a slow breath and drop your attention to your belly.
Ask, "What does my emotion mind want? What does my reasonable mind say?"
Breathe in and ask, "What does wise mind know?" Breathe out and listen.
Wait for the answer that feels calm, not urgent.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: Take a slow breath and drop your attention to your belly
What does your emotion mind want?
What does your reasonable mind say?
Breathe in, breathe out. What does wise mind know?
practice.hint: Wait for the answer that feels calm, not urgent.

skills.name: Observe, describe, participate
skills.what: DBT's core mindfulness skills: notice what's happening, put plain words to it, then take part fully, without judging yourself.
skills.when: When your mind is racing ahead or stuck in the past.
steps: Observe: notice one thing, like your breath, a sound or a sensation.
Describe: put it into words with no judgment. "My shoulders are tight."
Participate: throw yourself into one activity, like washing dishes or dancing.
When judgments show up, notice them and return to the facts.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: Observe: one thing you notice right now
practice.hint: Your breath, a sound, a sensation.

practice.label: Describe it with no judgment
practice.hint: "My shoulders are tight."

practice.label: Participate: what did you throw yourself into?
practice.hint: Washing dishes, dancing in the kitchen, folding clothes...

practice.label: Judgments that showed up
practice.hint: Notice them, then go back to the facts.

skills.name: STOP
skills.what: STOP is a quick pause for the moment right before you react.
skills.when: When you're about to snap, send the text or say the thing.
steps: S: Stop. Freeze for a moment.
T: Take a step back. Breathe.
O: Observe what's happening inside you and around you.
P: Proceed mindfully. Ask what will help, not what feels good right now.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: S: Stop. Freeze for a moment
T: Take a step back and breathe
O: What's happening inside you and around you?
P: What will actually help right now?
practice.hint: Not what feels good in the moment.

skills.name: TIPP
skills.what: TIPP changes your body chemistry to bring overwhelming emotions down fast.
skills.when: When an emotion is so strong you can't think straight.
steps: T: Temperature. Splash cold water on your face or hold something cold to your cheeks for 30 seconds.
I: Intense exercise. Move hard for a few minutes, like jumping jacks or a fast walk.
P: Paced breathing. Breathe out longer than you breathe in.
P: Paired muscle relaxation. Tense a muscle group while breathing in, then release as you breathe out.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press. Check with your doctor before using cold water if you have a heart condition.

practice.label: T: Cold water on your face or something cold on your cheeks for 30 seconds
I: Move hard for a few minutes
P: Breathe out longer than you breathe in
P: Tense a muscle while breathing in, release as you breathe out
Distress before and after, 0 to 10
practice.hint: Example: 8 before, 5 after.

skills.name: ACCEPTS
skills.what: ACCEPTS gives you ways to distract on purpose so you can get through a hard moment without making it worse.
skills.when: When you can't fix the problem right now and need to ride it out.
steps: Activities: do something that takes focus.
Contributing: help someone else.
Comparisons: remember a time you got through something hard.
Emotions: watch or listen to something that brings a different feeling.
Pushing away, Thoughts, Sensations: set it aside for now, count or name things, hold ice or take a warm shower.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: Which ones did you use?
practice.hint: Activities, Contributing, Comparisons, Emotions, Pushing away, Thoughts, Sensations

practice.label: How do you feel now?
practice.hint: A word or two is enough.

skills.name: Self-soothe with the five senses
skills.what: Self-soothing calms your body through what you see, hear, smell, taste and touch.
skills.when: When you feel raw, overwhelmed or alone.
steps: See: look at something calming, like photos, plants or the sky.
Hear: play music that steadies you.
Smell: light a candle or use lotion you love.
Taste: sip tea or eat something slowly.
Touch: wrap in a soft blanket or take a warm shower.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.
skills.lens: Self-soothing isn't something you have to earn. Many of us were taught that taking care of ourselves is selfish. It's maintenance.

practice.label: See
practice.hint: Photos, plants, the sky...

practice.label: Hear
practice.hint: A song that steadies you.

practice.label: Smell
practice.hint: A candle, lotion, shea butter...

practice.label: Taste
practice.hint: Tea, something you eat slowly.

practice.label: Touch
practice.hint: A soft blanket, a warm shower, your bonnet...

practice.label: How do you feel now?
practice.hint: A word or two is enough.

skills.name: Radical acceptance
skills.what: Radical acceptance means fully accepting what you can't change, so you stop spending energy fighting reality. It doesn't mean you approve of it.
skills.when: When you keep thinking "this shouldn't be happening" about something you can't control.
steps: Name what you're fighting: "I can't accept that..."
Remind yourself that this is what happened, and it has causes.
Notice where you hold the fight in your body and soften it.
Say, "It is what it is," and ask what you can do next.
Expect to repeat this. Acceptance often takes many tries.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.
skills.lens: Accepting that racism happened is not the same as accepting racism. Radical acceptance can free up energy for rest, healing or action.

practice.label: What you're fighting
practice.hint: "I can't accept that..."

practice.label: This is what happened, and it has causes
practice.hint: What were some of them?

practice.label: Where do you hold the fight in your body?
practice.hint: Soften it as you breathe.

practice.label: "It is what it is." What can you do next?
I know I may need to do this again. That's okay

skills.name: Check the facts
skills.what: Check whether your emotion, and how strong it is, fits the actual facts of the situation.
skills.when: When a feeling seems bigger than what happened.
steps: Name the emotion and its intensity.
Describe the event using only facts.
Ask what you're assuming or adding.
Ask whether the emotion and its size fit the facts. If they do, problem-solve. If not, try opposite action.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: The emotion and how strong it is (0 to 100)
What are you assuming or adding?
Does the emotion, and its size, fit the facts?
practice.hint: If yes, problem-solve. If not, try opposite action.

skills.name: Opposite action
skills.what: Every emotion comes with an urge. When the emotion doesn't fit the facts, acting opposite to the urge can change the feeling.
skills.when: When an emotion is pushing you to do something that won't help.
steps: Name the emotion and its urge, like shame and the urge to hide.
Check the facts. Does the emotion fit?
If not, do the opposite of the urge, all the way: reach out, show up, speak up.
Keep going until the emotion shifts.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: The emotion and its urge
practice.hint: Shame, and the urge to hide.

practice.label: Does the emotion fit the facts?
The opposite action you'll take, all the way
practice.hint: Reach out, show up, speak up.

practice.label: How did the emotion shift?
practice.hint: Come back and fill this in after.

skills.name: PLEASE
skills.what: PLEASE lowers your emotional vulnerability by caring for your body, so you're less likely to be knocked over by hard days.
skills.when: When you're more reactive than usual and can't figure out why.
steps: PL: Treat Physical iLlness. Take medications and get care when you're sick.
E: Eat regular, balanced meals.
A: Avoid mood-altering substances.
S: Sleep enough, on a steady schedule.
E: Exercise or move in some way most days.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: Took my meds or got care for anything physical
Which one needs the most love this week?

skills.name: Cope ahead
skills.what: Cope ahead is a mental rehearsal for a situation you know will be hard.
skills.when: Before a family holiday, a hard conversation, a doctor's visit or a big meeting.
steps: Describe the situation and the emotions you expect.
Choose the skills you'll use.
Picture the situation in detail, and picture yourself using the skills well.
Practice relaxing afterward.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: The situation coming up and the emotions you expect
practice.hint: Thanksgiving at your aunt's, a performance review...

practice.label: Picture it in detail. What do you see yourself doing well?

skills.name: DEAR MAN
skills.what: DEAR MAN helps you ask for what you need or say no clearly.
skills.when: When you need to make a request or set a limit.
steps: Describe the situation with facts. Express how you feel.
Assert what you want clearly. Reinforce: say why it helps them too.
Stay Mindful: keep returning to your point.
Appear confident, even if you don't feel it. Negotiate if it makes sense.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.
skills.lens: Many Black women worry that being direct will get them labeled angry or difficult. DEAR MAN gives you a calm structure, so your words carry the message.

practice.label: Express: how you feel
practice.hint: "I feel..."

practice.label: Assert: what you want
practice.hint: Say it clearly.

practice.label: Reinforce: why it helps them too
Mindful and Appear confident: your one-line point to come back to
Negotiate: what would you be willing to give?

skills.name: GIVE
skills.what: GIVE helps you keep a relationship strong while you have a hard conversation.
skills.when: When the relationship matters as much as the request.
steps: Be Gentle: no attacks, threats or judging.
Act Interested: listen and don't interrupt.
Validate: show you understand their side.
Use an Easy manner: a little warmth or humor.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: Gentle: how will you keep it gentle?
practice.hint: No attacks, threats or judging.

practice.label: Validate: what makes sense about their side?
Easy manner: a little warmth or humor you can bring

skills.name: FAST
skills.what: FAST helps you keep your self-respect in a conversation.
skills.when: When you tend to give in, over-apologize or bend your values to keep the peace.
steps: Be Fair to yourself and the other person.
No extra Apologies for having a need or an opinion.
Stick to your values.
Be Truthful. Don't exaggerate or make excuses.
skills.source: Linehan, M. M. (2015). DBT skills training manual (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: What's the request or the stand you're taking?
Fair: what's fair to you and to them?
No extra apologies for having a need
Stick to values: which value is this about?
Truthful: your honest version, no excuses

skills.name: Box breathing
skills.what: Box breathing slows your breath to an even rhythm, which tells your body it's safe.
skills.when: When you feel anxious, before a stressful moment, or when you can't sleep.
steps: Breathe in for 4 counts.
Hold for 4 counts.
Breathe out for 4 counts.
Rest for 4 counts.
Repeat for 1 to 3 minutes.
skills.source: Zaccaro, A., et al. (2018). How breath-control can change your life: A systematic review on psycho-physiological correlates of slow breathing. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 12, 353.

practice.label: How do you feel now?
practice.hint: A word or two is enough.

skills.name: The physiological sigh
skills.what: Two quick inhales followed by one long exhale. In one study, people who did this for 5 minutes a day saw bigger mood boosts than people who did mindfulness meditation.
skills.when: When you need to calm down in under a minute.
steps: Breathe in through your nose.
Without breathing out, take a second short breath in to fill your lungs.
Breathe out slowly through your mouth until your lungs are empty.
Repeat 2 or 3 times.
skills.source: Balban, M. Y., et al. (2023). Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal. Cell Reports Medicine, 4(1), 100895.

practice.label: Take a second short breath in to fill your lungs
Breathe out slowly through your mouth
How do you feel now?
practice.hint: A word or two is enough.

skills.name: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
skills.what: Grounding uses your senses to pull your mind back to the present when anxiety, panic or memories take over.
skills.when: During a panic attack, a trigger or when you feel disconnected from your body.
steps: Name 5 things you can see.
Name 4 things you can feel.
Name 3 things you can hear.
Name 2 things you can smell.
Name 1 thing you can taste.
skills.source: Najavits, L. M. (2002). Seeking safety: A treatment manual for PTSD and substance abuse. Guilford Press.

practice.label: How do you feel now?
practice.hint: A word or two is enough.

skills.name: Progressive muscle relaxation
skills.what: Tensing and releasing your muscles one group at a time teaches your body the difference between tense and relaxed.
skills.when: When stress lives in your shoulders, jaw or stomach, or when you can't fall asleep.
steps: Sit or lie down comfortably.
Tense your feet for 5 seconds, then release for 10.
Move up your body: legs, stomach, hands, arms, shoulders, face.
Notice the difference after each release.
skills.source: Jacobson, E. (1938). Progressive relaxation. University of Chicago Press.

practice.label: Where did you notice the biggest difference?

skills.name: Urge surfing
skills.what: Urges rise, peak and fall like a wave. Urge surfing means riding the wave without acting on it.
skills.when: When you feel pulled to binge, scroll, text an ex, drink or seek reassurance.
steps: Notice the urge and name it.
Find where you feel it in your body.
Breathe and watch it like a wave: rising, peaking, falling.
Set a timer for 10 minutes. Most urges ease by then.
Notice that you can feel an urge without obeying it.
skills.source: Bowen, S., & Marlatt, A. (2009). Surfing the urge: Brief mindfulness-based intervention for college student smokers. Psychology of Addictive Behaviors, 23(4), 666–671.

practice.label: The urge
practice.hint: To text him, to scroll, to snap, to eat when you're not hungry...

practice.label: Where do you feel it in your body?
Set a 10-minute timer and watch the wave rise, peak and fall
How strong was it at the start and at the end? (0 to 10)
What did you notice?
practice.hint: You can feel an urge without obeying it.

skills.name: Name it to tame it
skills.what: Putting a feeling into words can turn down the brain's alarm response. Researchers call it affect labeling.
skills.when: When a feeling hits hard and fast.
steps: Pause and ask, "What am I feeling?"
Name it in one or two words: "anxious," "embarrassed," "left out."
Say it out loud or write it down.
Notice whether the intensity shifts, even slightly.
skills.source: Lieberman, M. D., et al. (2007). Putting feelings into words: Affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli. Psychological Science, 18(5), 421–428.

practice.label: What are you feeling?
practice.hint: One or two words: anxious, embarrassed, left out.

practice.label: Did the intensity shift, even a little?

skills.name: Leaves on a stream
skills.what: A mindfulness exercise from acceptance and commitment therapy that helps you watch thoughts without getting pulled in.
skills.when: When you're overthinking, ruminating or can't shut your mind off at night.
steps: Close your eyes and picture a gentle stream with leaves floating by.
Each time a thought comes, place it on a leaf.
Watch it float away. Don't push it or hold it.
If you get pulled in, notice that, and gently start again.
skills.source: Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (2012). Acceptance and commitment therapy (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: Close your eyes and picture a gentle stream
Thoughts you placed on leaves
practice.hint: Write a few if you'd like.

practice.label: Did you get pulled in? What pulled you?
practice.hint: Noticing it is the practice.

practice.label: How do you feel now?
practice.hint: A word or two is enough.

skills.name: Body scan
skills.what: A slow scan from head to toe that helps you notice stress your body is holding.
skills.when: When you feel disconnected from your body or worn down.
steps: Lie down or sit comfortably.
Bring attention to the top of your head.
Move slowly down: face, neck, shoulders, arms, chest, belly, legs, feet.
Notice each area without trying to fix it. Breathe into tight spots.
skills.source: Kabat-Zinn, J. (1990). Full catastrophe living. Delacorte.
skills.lens: Many Black women carry stress in their bodies for years. A body scan is one way to notice what you've been holding.

practice.label: Where were the tight spots?
practice.hint: Just notice. No fixing needed.

skills.name: Body doubling
skills.what: Working alongside another person, in the room or on video, can make it easier to start and stick with a task.
skills.when: When you keep putting off a task you can't seem to start alone.
steps: Pick the task and how long you'll work.
Invite a friend, or join a virtual co-working session.
Say out loud what you'll work on.
Work side by side. You don't have to talk.
Share what you got done at the end.
skills.source: A common ADHD coaching strategy. Research on it is still early.

practice.label: The task and how long you'll work
Who's your body double?
practice.hint: A friend on FaceTime, a co-working session, your sister on the couch...

practice.label: What you said you'd work on
What you got done
practice.hint: Share it with them at the end.

skills.name: The tiny first step
skills.what: Big tasks can freeze an ADHD or depressed brain. Shrinking the first step until it's almost too easy helps you start.
skills.when: When a task feels so big you can't begin.
steps: Name the task.
Ask, "What's the very first physical action?" Like "open the laptop."
Make it smaller if it still feels hard.
Do only that step. Keep going if you want to.
Plan when and where: "At 7 p.m., at the kitchen table, I'll open the laptop."
skills.source: Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist, 54(7), 493–503.

practice.label: The very first physical action
practice.hint: "Open the laptop."

practice.label: Smaller, if it still feels hard
When and where
practice.hint: "At 7 p.m., at the kitchen table."

skills.name: Make time visible
skills.what: Time blindness makes time hard to feel. Visual tools turn time into something you can see.
skills.when: When you're often late, lose hours or underestimate how long things take.
steps: Use a visual timer that shows time shrinking.
Before a task, guess how long it will take. Time it, then compare.
Set alarms for when to leave, not just when to arrive.
Put clocks where you'll see them.
skills.source: Barkley, R. A. (1997). Behavioral inhibition, sustained attention, and executive functions: Constructing a unifying theory of ADHD. Psychological Bulletin, 121(1), 65–94.

practice.label: Your guess: how long will it take?
How long did it actually take?
practice.hint: Compare. No judgment.

practice.label: Your leave-by time and alarm
practice.hint: Set it for when to leave, not when to arrive.

skills.name: Brain dump
skills.what: Write down every task, worry and to-do in your head. Research shows that making a plan for unfinished tasks frees up your mind.
skills.when: When your mind feels crowded or you can't focus.
steps: Set a timer for 10 minutes.
Write everything in your head, in any order.
Sort each item: now, later, or not mine.
Pick one "now" item and schedule it.
skills.source: Masicampo, E. J., & Baumeister, R. F. (2011). Consider it done! Plan making can eliminate the cognitive effects of unfulfilled goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 101(4), 667–683.

practice.label: Everything in your head (10 minutes)
practice.hint: Any order. Don't edit.

practice.label: Not mine
practice.hint: Things that belong to someone else.

practice.label: The one "now" item and when you'll do it

skills.name: Sensory toolkit
skills.what: A sensory toolkit is a set of items that calms your senses when the world gets too loud, bright or busy.
skills.when: Before or during sensory overload, like church, cookouts, offices or stores.
steps: Notice what overloads you: noise, light, crowds, textures or smells.
Pack tools that help: earplugs or headphones, sunglasses, a soft texture, a calming scent, a snack.
Plan an exit spot, like your car or a quiet room.
Use it early, before overload builds.
skills.source: Raymaker, D. M., et al. (2020). "Having all of your internal resources exhausted beyond measure and being left with no clean-up crew": Defining autistic burnout. Autism in Adulthood, 2(2), 132–143.

practice.label: What overloads you?
practice.hint: Noise, light, crowds, textures, smells...

practice.label: Your toolkit
practice.hint: Earbuds, sunglasses, a soft texture, a calming scent, a snack...

practice.label: Your exit spot
practice.hint: Your car, a bathroom, a quiet room.

practice.label: Where will you use it early this week?
practice.hint: Before overload builds.

skills.name: Energy budgeting
skills.what: Treat your energy like a budget. Some activities cost more, including masking. Planning around your energy helps prevent burnout.
skills.when: When you keep running out of energy before the week is over.
steps: List this week's activities.
Rate the energy each one costs: low, medium or high. Count masking and travel too.
Add recharge activities that give energy back.
Move or drop something if the week is over budget.
skills.source: Raymaker, D. M., et al. (2020). "Having all of your internal resources exhausted beyond measure and being left with no clean-up crew": Defining autistic burnout. Autism in Adulthood, 2(2), 132–143.

practice.label: This week's activities with an energy cost (low, medium, high)
practice.hint: Count masking, code-switching and travel too.

practice.label: What will you move or drop if you're over budget?

skills.name: Meltdown and shutdown plan
skills.what: A plan written when you're calm, for the moments overload takes over.
skills.when: Make it on a good day. Use it when you notice early signs.
steps: Write your early signs, like irritability, going quiet or noise feeling painful.
List what helps: a dark room, pressure, quiet, being alone.
List what doesn't help, like questions or touch.
Share the plan with one or two trusted people.
skills.source: Raymaker, D. M., et al. (2020). "Having all of your internal resources exhausted beyond measure and being left with no clean-up crew": Defining autistic burnout. Autism in Adulthood, 2(2), 132–143.

practice.label: Your early signs
practice.hint: Irritability, going quiet, noise feeling painful...

practice.label: What helps
practice.hint: A dark room, pressure, quiet, being alone.

practice.label: What doesn't help
practice.hint: Questions, touch...

practice.label: Who will you share this plan with?

skills.name: Unmasking moments
skills.what: Masking and code-switching take energy. Choosing safe times to stop can lower stress and burnout.
skills.when: When you feel exhausted from performing all day.
steps: Notice when you mask or code-switch most.
Name one or two people or places where you can be yourself.
Schedule time there each week.
Notice how your body feels after.
skills.source: Hull, L., et al. (2017). "Putting on my best normal": Social camouflaging in adults with autism spectrum conditions. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 47(8), 2519–2534.
skills.lens: Black autistic women often mask twice: to fit in as neurotypical and to stay safe in white spaces. You deserve places where you don't have to do either.

practice.label: When do you mask or code-switch the most?
People or places where you can be fully yourself
When will you spend time there this week?
How did your body feel after?
practice.hint: Come back and fill this in.

skills.name: The boundary script
skills.what: A simple 3-part script for setting a limit without a long explanation.
skills.when: When someone keeps crossing a line.
steps: Name what happens: "When you comment on my weight..."
Name the impact: "...I feel hurt..."
Name what you'll do: "...so I'm going to change the subject or leave."
Follow through, calmly.
skills.source: Speed, B. C., Goldstein, B. L., & Goldfried, M. R. (2018). Assertiveness training: A forgotten evidence-based treatment. Clinical Psychology: Science and Practice, 25(1), e12216.

practice.label: When you...
practice.hint: "When you comment on my weight at family dinner..."

practice.label: I feel...
practice.hint: "...I feel hurt..."

practice.label: So I'm going to...
practice.hint: "...so I'm going to change the subject or leave."

practice.label: How did following through go?
practice.hint: Come back and fill this in after.

skills.name: The broken record
skills.what: Repeat your no calmly, without adding new reasons each time someone pushes.
skills.when: When someone won't take no for an answer.
steps: Pick one short sentence: "I'm not able to do that."
When they push, repeat it, word for word.
Skip new explanations. They give the other person more to argue with.
End the conversation if you need to.
skills.source: Speed, B. C., Goldstein, B. L., & Goldfried, M. R. (2018). Assertiveness training: A forgotten evidence-based treatment. Clinical Psychology: Science and Practice, 25(1), e12216.

practice.label: Your one short sentence
practice.hint: "I'm not able to do that."

practice.label: I repeated it word for word, no new explanations

skills.name: Repair after conflict
skills.what: Repair is how relationships recover after a fight. It matters more than never fighting at all.
skills.when: After an argument with a partner, child, friend or family member.
steps: Wait until you're both calm.
Own your part: "I raised my voice, and that wasn't okay."
Name the impact: "I know that hurt."
Say what you'll do differently.
Listen to their side without defending.
skills.source: Gottman, J. M., & Silver, N. (1999). The seven principles for making marriage work. Crown.

practice.label: Your part
practice.hint: "I raised my voice, and that wasn't okay."

practice.label: The impact
practice.hint: "I know that hurt."

practice.label: What you heard from their side
practice.hint: Listen without defending.

skills.name: Self-compassion break
skills.what: A short practice for treating yourself with the kindness you'd give a friend. Research links self-compassion with less anxiety and depression.
skills.when: When you're hurting, ashamed or criticizing yourself.
steps: Name it: "This is a moment of pain."
Remember you're not alone: "Other women feel this too."
Place a hand on your heart.
Say, "May I be kind to myself right now."
skills.source: Neff, K. D., & Germer, C. K. (2013). A pilot study and randomized controlled trial of the mindful self-compassion program. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 69(1), 28–44.
skills.lens: If kindness toward yourself feels unfamiliar or even uncomfortable, that makes sense. Many of us were raised to push through. You can practice this anyway.

practice.label: This is a moment of pain. What's hurting?
Other women feel this too. I'm not alone
Your kind words to yourself
practice.hint: "May I be kind to myself right now."

skills.name: Values check
skills.what: Values are what matter most to you. Checking choices against them makes decisions clearer.
skills.when: When you're facing a big choice or feel pulled by other people's expectations.
steps: Write your top 5 values, like family, freedom, faith, rest or creativity.
Pick the 3 that matter most right now.
For a decision, ask, "Which option moves me toward these?"
Take one small step in that direction this week.
skills.source: Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (2012). Acceptance and commitment therapy (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

practice.label: Your top 5 values
practice.hint: Family, faith, freedom, rest, creativity...

practice.label: The 3 that matter most right now
The decision in front of you, and which option moves you toward them

skills.name: The evidence file
skills.what: A running record of your wins, praise and growth, for when impostor feelings tell you otherwise.
skills.when: Before reviews, interviews, big meetings, or when self-doubt is loud.
steps: Make a folder or note called "Evidence."
Save praise emails, results, thank-you notes and goals you've met.
Add one entry each week.
Read it when you start doubting yourself.
skills.source: Clance, P. R., & Imes, S. A. (1978). The impostor phenomenon in high achieving women. Psychotherapy: Theory, Research & Practice, 15(3), 241–247.

practice.label: This week's entry
practice.hint: Praise, a result, a thank-you note, a goal you met.

practice.label: Something from your past you're proud of
Read it back. What do you notice?

skills.name: Rest menu
skills.what: A short list of rest options by time, so rest is easy to choose even when you're exhausted.
skills.when: When you have time to rest but don't know how to use it.
steps: Write 3 rest options that take 5 minutes, like stretching or stepping outside.
Write 3 that take 30 minutes, like a nap or a bath.
Write 3 for a whole day, like a day with no plans.
Keep the list on your phone. Pick one when you get the chance.
skills.source: Hersey, T. (2022). Rest is resistance: A manifesto. Little, Brown Spark.
skills.lens: Writer and activist Tricia Hersey calls rest a form of resistance for Black people, who were long denied it. Rest isn't a reward for finishing. It's a need.

practice.label: 3 rest options that take 5 minutes
practice.hint: Stretching, stepping outside, a song with your eyes closed...

practice.label: 3 that take 30 minutes
practice.hint: A nap, a bath, a walk...

practice.label: 3 for a whole day
practice.hint: A day with no plans.

skills.name: Letter to someone you lost
skills.what: Writing about loss can help you process feelings that are hard to say out loud. Research on expressive writing links it to better health and mood.
skills.when: On anniversaries, hard days, or when grief feels stuck.
steps: Set aside 15 to 20 minutes.
Write to the person, pregnancy or version of life you lost.
Say what you miss, what you wish, what you never got to say.
Keep it, burn it or read it to someone you trust.
skills.source: Pennebaker, J. W., & Beall, S. K. (1986). Confronting a traumatic event: Toward an understanding of inhibition and disease. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 95(3), 274–281.

practice.label: Who or what you're writing to
practice.hint: A person, a pregnancy, a version of life you lost.

practice.label: Your letter
practice.hint: What you miss, what you wish, what you never got to say. Take 15 to 20 minutes.

practice.label: What you'll do with it
practice.hint: Keep it, burn it, or read it to someone you trust.

skills.name: Energy audit
skills.what: A quick look at what drains you and what refills you, so you can make one small trade.
skills.when: When you feel burned out but can't tell what's causing it.
steps: Draw two columns: drains and refills.
List everything from this week in one column or the other.
Circle the biggest drain you have some control over.
Trade it for one refill this week, even partly.
skills.source: Maslach, C., & Leiter, M. P. (2016). Understanding the burnout experience: Recent research and its implications for psychiatry. World Psychiatry, 15(2), 103–111.

practice.label: The biggest drain you have some control over
The refill you'll trade it for
practice.hint: Even partly counts.
